title: A history of pirates

paragraphs.text: In May 1724, a new book appeared in Charles Rivington's shop in London. It was a small book with a plain leather cover and must have appeared rather dull compared to the finely bound volumes with embossed gold-leaf lettering that filled the shelves. The author, Captain Charles Johnson, was not well known and the book would surely have passed unnoticed if it had not been for the arresting title: A History of the Most Notorious Pirates. Captain Johnson's History was topical because there had been an alarming increase in pirate attacks during the previous years, and there is archive evidence to suggest that British newspapers at the time were filled with accounts of piracy and pirate trials. Sales receipts have been lost, but it would appear certain that the book immediately found favour with the reading public because within a few months a second edition was published and more soon followed. It has been said, and there seems no reason to question this, that Captain Johnson created the modern conception of pirates. He provided a sweeping account of what came to be known as the 'Golden Age of Piracy' and it was here that his legacy was born. Johnson gave an almost mythical status to the more colourful pirates such as Blackbeard, and inspired later generations of writers and film-makers, who adapted elements of his stories.

One of the first works of fiction to draw on Johnson's work was Sir Walter Scott's novel The Pirate, an epic saga that was based only loosely on the life of the real pirate John Gow. The novel was popular in its day, but like many of the other historical novels by Scott it has struggled to maintain its reputation with the modern reader. This is not the case with Robert Louis Stevenson's classic novel Treasure Island, which has some claim to being the greatest of all pirate stories. What's more, much of the detail in Treasure Island is correct.

Numerous seamen like Ben Gunn were marooned on desert islands by pirates, and there are several authenticated accounts of one-legged pirates like Long John Silver. But it was rare for pirates to bury their treasure, and Robert Louis Stevenson seems to have invented the idea of the pirates' treasure map. In more recent times many films have had a tendency to borrow from Johnson's History, without being too concerned about historical accuracy. The elegantly choreographed sword fights of pirate movies are a far cry from reality, and most Hollywood stars are chosen for their dashing good looks. This should not lessen the appeal of the films, which are unashamedly intended as popular entertainment rather than historical record, but it has tended to give a fictitious air to all stories about pirates.

What has become clear over the years is that the majority of facts in Johnson's History have been proved remarkably accurate, though there are a few notable exceptions. It seems likely that when he introduces conversation into his biographies he uses considerable license. A question mark must also hang over his account of the early lives of the women pirates, Mary Read and Anne Bonny. But it is amazing how every detail of Johnson's lengthy biographies of the pirates Bartholomew Roberts, Blackbeard, Major Stede Bonnet and John Rackam stand up to scrutiny against the historical records.

Given the success of Johnson's History, it is curious that the identity of the author has proved so elusive. He seems to have attracted little attention during his lifetime, and no obituaries of Captain Charles Johnson have ever been found in any newspapers from that time, so it seems likely that his name was an assumed one. It is improbable that Charles Rivington, the publisher of the first edition of the book, was really Captain Johnson, because he never travelled outside London, where he dedicated himself to building up the fortunes of the publishing company that he founded. A far more convincing candidate for the authorship of the History is the writer Daniel Defoe. The case for Defoe was first made in 1932 by the American scholar John Moore. Most significantly, Defoe spent much of his colourful life making journeys all around the world, and especially to those islands where many pirates had lived.

But then in 1998 two scholars from New York University challenged Moore's theory. Though there was little doubt Moore was an expert on Defoe, they questioned the reliability of his scholarship, in particular his practice of building one argument on top of another and ignoring the fact there was no logical connection between them. This leaves us still unclear regarding Captain Johnson's identity, and all we can do is speculate as to what sort of man he was. What does seem possible is that the writer of the History may actually have been a pirate himself, partly because he sometimes shows an admiration for the pirates and an understanding of their lifestyles that few other people at that time would have felt. Furthermore, there seems little doubt that the author was a seaman of some experience, for it is abundantly clear that he understood the workings of the ships he describes. But for the time being his real name must remain a mystery.
